set.detail: The Roman-Parthian war of 58-63 over Armenia was the major eastern conflict of Nero's reign. When Vologases I installed his brother Tiridates as king of Armenia in 52-54, exploiting the chaos after Radamistus's usurpation, Nero sent Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo to command in Cappadocia and Galatia. Corbulo spent several years retraining the eastern legions, which Tacitus describes as slack from long peace, wintering them in tents in the Armenian highlands where sentries froze to death, and executing deserters. In 58 he invaded Armenia, taking fortresses by assault and accepting the surrender of Artaxata, which he burned, and in 59 marched to Tigranocerta, which opened its gates. Nero installed Tigranes VI, a Cappadocian prince raised in Rome, as king in 60, with Roman troops in support, and Corbulo became governor of Syria. Tigranes's invasion of Adiabene provoked Vologases to send an army that besieged Tigranocerta in 61; a truce followed, and Armenia was to be referred to Nero. In 62 Lucius Caesennius Paetus, sent to command in Armenia and boasting he would make it a province, divided his forces, was surrounded at Rhandeia on the Arsanias and capitulated, agreeing to withdraw from Armenia, with his troops passing under the yoke according to rumour, while Corbulo was slow to help. In 63 Corbulo, given maius imperium over the eastern provinces, invaded Armenia again with four legions, and Tiridates met him at Rhandeia, laying his diadem before Nero's statue. The compromise, by which an Arsacid prince would rule Armenia but receive his crown from Rome, was sealed in Rome in 66 with Tiridates's coronation by Nero, celebrated with the closing of the temple of Janus. The settlement held for fifty years until Trajan's Parthian war. Tacitus's account (Annals 13-15), drawing on Corbulo's memoirs, is detailed but favourable to Corbulo and hostile to Paetus.

The First Jewish-Roman War (66-74) began with the revolt in Jerusalem in 66, provoked by the procurator Gessius Florus's seizure of Temple funds and massacres, the cessation of the sacrifice for the emperor, the massacre of the Roman garrison and the defeat of the Syrian legate Cestius Gallus at Beth Horon. A provisional government in Jerusalem led by the former High Priest Ananus son of Ananus organised the defence, sending commanders including Josephus to Galilee. Nero appointed Vespasian in 67 with three legions (V Macedonica, X Fretensis and XV Apollinaris, joined by Titus) and allied troops, some 60,000 men. Vespasian conquered Galilee in 67, taking Jotapata after a 47-day siege, where Josephus surrendered, Tarichaeae with a battle on the Sea of Galilee, Gamala and Gischala, whose commander John escaped to Jerusalem. In 68 he subdued Peraea, Idumaea and the coast, and isolated Jerusalem, but suspended operations after Nero's death. In Jerusalem the factions fought each other: the Zealots, with Idumaean help, killed Ananus and other moderates; John of Gischala, Simon bar Giora and Eleazar ben Simon fought for control. After Vespasian's proclamation in 69, Titus besieged Jerusalem from April to September 70 and destroyed the city and Temple. The triumph of 71 displayed the Temple treasures; Simon was executed. The war was concluded by the governors Lucilius Bassus and Flavius Silva, who took Herodium, Machaerus and finally Masada (73 or 74). The consequences were profound: the Temple cult ended, the high priesthood and Sanhedrin disappeared, the Jewish tax for the Temple was transferred to Jupiter Capitolinus as the fiscus Judaicus, X Fretensis was stationed in Jerusalem, and rabbinic Judaism began to develop at Yavneh. Josephus's Jewish War, written by a participant who changed sides, is the main source, with Tacitus's fragmentary Histories 5 and Dio.

The civil wars of 68-70, the "year of the four emperors", followed the collapse of Nero's regime. In March 68 Gaius Julius Vindex, governor of Lugdunensis, rebelled and invited Galba, governor of Tarraconensis, to take power; Galba was proclaimed by his troops on 2 April. Vindex was defeated by the Rhine legions under Verginius Rufus at Vesontio in May, but the praetorians deserted Nero, who killed himself in June. Galba, 71, arrived in Rome in autumn, executed opponents, refused the donative promised in his name ("I choose soldiers, I do not buy them") and adopted the aristocrat Piso Licinianus. On 1 January 69 the legions of Upper Germany refused allegiance and on 2 January the Lower German legions proclaimed their governor Vitellius. On 15 January Otho, who had hoped to be adopted, had the praetorians murder Galba and Piso in the Forum. Vitellius's generals Fabius Valens and Caecina Alienus invaded Italy, and defeated Otho's forces at the first battle of Bedriacum near Cremona on 14 April; Otho killed himself on 16 April to avoid further bloodshed. Vitellius entered Rome in July, replacing the praetorians with his German legionaries. Meanwhile the eastern armies proclaimed Vespasian (1 July), and the Danube legions under Antonius Primus invaded Italy, defeated the Vitellians at the second battle of Bedriacum on 24-25 October and sacked Cremona for four days. In Rome Vespasian's brother Flavius Sabinus tried to negotiate Vitellius's abdication, but was besieged on the Capitol, which burned on 19 December, and killed; the Flavian army stormed Rome on 20 December, killing Vitellius after a final battle in the streets. The Batavian revolt and Gallic secession continued into 70. Tacitus's Histories, Plutarch's Galba and Otho, Suetonius and Dio are the sources. The wars revealed, in Tacitus's phrase, that an emperor could be made elsewhere than at Rome.

The Batavian revolt (69-70) began as a part of the civil war and became a rebellion of Germanic and Gallic peoples. The Batavi of the Rhine delta, exempted from tribute in return for supplying elite auxiliary troops, were alienated by Vitellius's heavy recruitment. Julius Civilis, a Batavian noble and Roman citizen who had served 25 years as an auxiliary commander, had been sent in chains to Nero and acquitted by Galba; in 69, ostensibly supporting Vespasian at the request of Antonius Primus, he raised the Batavi, Cananefates and Frisii, was joined by eight Batavian cohorts returning from Italy, and with the support of Germanic tribes across the Rhine besieged the double legionary fortress of Vetera. The prophetess Veleda of the Bructeri foretold the destruction of the legions. After Vitellius's death the revolt continued; Roman troops murdered their commander Hordeonius Flaccus, and in early 70 Vetera surrendered and its garrison was massacred after leaving under a promise of safety. The Treveri and Lingones under Julius Classicus, Julius Tutor and Julius Sabinus proclaimed an "Empire of the Gauls" (Imperium Galliarum), and the legions in Germany swore allegiance to it, the lowest point of Roman military history according to Tacitus. A Gallic council at Durocortorum (Reims) refused to join, preferring Roman rule. Vespasian sent Petillius Cerialis with eight legions; he defeated the Treveri at Rigodulum, recovered Trier and Cologne, won a hard battle at Vetera, and campaigned in the Batavian island until Civilis negotiated a surrender in autumn 70; the text of Tacitus breaks off during the parley. The Batavi kept their privileges, and the legions that had sworn to the Gallic empire were disbanded or reformed. Julius Sabinus hid for nine years in a tomb with his wife Epponina before being executed. Tacitus (Histories 4-5) is the only detailed source; modern scholars debate whether Civilis aimed at independence or at power within the Roman system.
set.debate: Whether Civilis sought independence or used the civil war to gain power within the Roman system.

set.detail: Domitian's war against the Chatti (83-85) was the first major campaign of his reign and the only one he led in person against the Germans. The Chatti of the Hessian uplands, the most warlike Germanic people near the Rhine according to Tacitus, raided across the river. In spring 83 Domitian went to the Rhine on the pretext of conducting a census in Gaul, and with forces drawn from several legions and vexillations from Britain attacked the Chatti from Mogontiacum. Frontinus, who served in the campaign, describes how Domitian drove roads 120 miles long through the forests to expose their hiding places and compensated landowners for land used for forts. The campaign took the Taunus mountains and the Wetterau, which were annexed and protected by a line of watchtowers and forts linked by a patrol road, the beginning of the Upper German limes. Domitian took the title Germanicus and celebrated a triumph in 83, and coins proclaimed GERMANIA CAPTA. Tacitus, Pliny and Dio mocked the victory as a sham, Tacitus claiming that Domitian bought slaves to impersonate captives. Fighting continued in 84-85, and a new legion, I Minervia, was raised. At about the same time the two military zones on the Rhine were organised as the provinces of Germania Superior and Inferior. The war's outcome, the shortening of the frontier between Rhine and Danube and control of the fertile Wetterau, was a real strategic gain, and modern historians (Jones) consider the hostile verdict of the senatorial sources unjustified. A Chattan threat recurred in 89, when the Chatti supported the revolt of Saturninus but were prevented from crossing the Rhine by a sudden thaw.

Domitian's Dacian war (85-89) was the first great conflict with the kingdom that Decebalus would lead. In winter 85/86 the Dacians crossed the frozen Danube into Moesia and killed the governor Gaius Oppius Sabinus. Domitian came to the Danube with the praetorian prefect Cornelius Fuscus, who drove the Dacians out; Moesia was divided into Superior and Inferior. In 86 or 87 Fuscus crossed into Dacia with a large army and was killed in an ambush, losing a legion (probably V Alaudae) and its eagle; the Adamclisi altar may commemorate the dead of this or a later battle. In 88 Tettius Julianus, legate of Moesia Superior, invaded Dacia through the Iron Gates and won a major victory at Tapae, where the Dacian commander Vezinas escaped by feigning death. Decebalus, who had become king in place of Duras, sued for peace. Domitian, distracted by the revolt of Saturninus in Upper Germany (January 89) and by the hostility of the Marcomanni and Quadi, who had refused help, accepted a settlement in 89: Decebalus's brother Diegis received a diadem from Domitian as a sign of Decebalus's client status, and Rome paid subsidies and sent engineers and craftsmen. Domitian celebrated a triumph and took the title Dacicus. The senatorial tradition (Dio, Pliny) presented the treaty as a humiliating peace bought with gold, which Trajan later invoked to justify his wars. Modern historians see it as a reasonable arrangement that secured the lower Danube while Domitian dealt with the Suebi and Sarmatians. The war led to the build-up of legions on the Danube, which by the end of Domitian's reign held nine legions, and to a series of military reforms. Dio's epitome, Suetonius, Jordanes and inscriptions are the main sources, with gaps and uncertainties in chronology.
set.debate: Date of Fuscus's defeat (86 or 87) and the identity of the lost legion.

set.detail: The Suebic-Sarmatian war (89-97) was fought on the middle Danube against the Marcomanni and Quadi (Suebi) and the Sarmatian Iazyges. In 89, during the Dacian war, the Marcomanni and Quadi refused to provide troops, and Domitian attacked them, without success; he executed their envoys. In 92 the Iazyges and Suebi invaded Pannonia and destroyed legio XXI Rapax with its legate, one of the few complete legionary losses of the period. Domitian went to the Danube for eight months and won a victory, for which he celebrated only an ovation (not a triumph) and dedicated a laurel crown to Jupiter Capitolinus. Fighting continued intermittently; an inscription records a "Suebic war" (bellum Suebicum) in 97 under Nerva, for which Nerva and Trajan took the title Germanicus after a victory announced in autumn 97, shortly before Trajan's adoption. The war is poorly documented, known from brief notices in Dio and Suetonius, the poems of Martial and Statius and inscriptions of officers decorated for service. Its importance lies in the redeployment of the army to the middle and lower Danube, the creation of new legionary bases at Aquincum, Brigetio and later Vindobona, and the developing understanding of the Danube as the empire's principal frontier. It anticipated the Marcomannic wars of Marcus Aurelius, fought against the same peoples on the same front seventy years later. Dio says that Domitian's difficulties led him to conclude the Dacian peace on unfavourable terms; modern historians (Jones, Strobel) see a coherent policy of defending the Danube by diplomacy and force. The legion XXI Rapax, previously at Vindonissa and Mogontiacum, had been transferred to Pannonia after supporting Saturninus.

The First Dacian War (101-102) was launched by Trajan to end the Domitianic settlement with Decebalus, whose kingdom in the Carpathian arc had grown strong with Roman subsidies and engineers. Trajan prepared carefully: he improved the Danube road through the Iron Gates (completed 100) and built a canal to bypass the cataracts (101). In spring 101 he crossed the Danube on pontoon bridges at Lederata and Dierna with perhaps nine legions and large auxiliary forces, accompanied by Hadrian and Licinius Sura, and advanced towards Sarmizegetusa Regia, the Dacian royal centre in the Orastie mountains. At Tapae, a hard-fought battle in a storm left many Roman wounded, and Trajan tore up his own clothes for bandages. Decebalus sent a mushroom with a Latin message from the Buri urging peace. In winter 101/102 the Dacians and their Roxolani allies counter-attacked across the lower Danube into Moesia Inferior, and Trajan defeated them in a battle commemorated by the altar and Tropaeum at Adamclisi, with heavy Roman losses (3,800 names on the altar, possibly from this or an earlier battle). In 102 Trajan pressed through the mountains, taking fortresses and recovering the eagle lost by Fuscus; Laberius Maximus captured Decebalus's sister, and Decebalus surrendered. Under the peace he gave up territory and siege engines, handed over Roman deserters and engineers, demolished fortresses, and accepted client status. Trajan took the title Dacicus and celebrated a triumph in late 102. Roman garrisons remained in parts of Dacia, and Apollodorus began the bridge at Drobeta. The narrative is reconstructed from Dio's epitome, the reliefs of Trajan's Column, inscriptions and archaeology of Roman and Dacian fortresses, but the order of events and the location of the battles are debated.
set.debate: Location of the battles and whether the Adamclisi altar commemorates the dead of 102 or of Domitian's war.

set.detail: The Second Dacian War (105-106) ended the Dacian kingdom. Decebalus rebuilt his fortresses, acquired arms, received Roman deserters and attacked the Iazyges, Rome's allies, violating the treaty of 102, and the Senate declared war in 105. Decebalus captured the commander Pompeius Longinus by treachery, who poisoned himself, and sent deserters to assassinate Trajan in Moesia; Dacians attacked Roman garrisons north of the Danube. Trajan left Rome in June 105 and crossed the Danube on Apollodorus's great stone and timber bridge at Drobeta, with some fourteen legions or detachments. In 106 Roman armies converged on Sarmizegetusa Regia, which fell after a siege; Dacian nobles poisoned themselves, and the city was burned. Decebalus fled north towards the Carpathians and, when overtaken by a cavalry patrol under Tiberius Claudius Maximus, cut his own throat; his head was displayed in Rome. His companion Bicilis revealed the location of his treasure in the river Sargetia. Dacia was annexed as a province with Decimus Terentius Scaurianus as first governor, the colony of Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa was founded, two legions (IV Flavia Felix, then XIII Gemina at Apulum) were stationed, and colonists were brought in from across the empire, especially Illyrian miners for the gold mines. The spoils financed the games of 107 and Trajan's building programme in Rome, including the Forum and Column. Coins proclaimed DACIA CAPTA. The war is depicted in the second half of the Column's frieze. The annexation brought Roman rule north of the lower Danube for 165 years until Aurelian's withdrawal (c. 271-275). The question of continuity of the Daco-Roman population after the withdrawal has been central to Romanian national history. Dio's account survives only in excerpts, and Trajan's own commentaries (Dacica) are lost except for one sentence.

Trajan's Parthian war (113-117) was the most ambitious eastern war in Roman history. The pretext was the Parthian king Osroes's deposition of the Armenian king Axidares and installation of his nephew Parthamasiris without Roman consent, breaking the Rhandeia settlement. Trajan left Rome in October 113, refused Osroes's embassy at Athens, and in 114 marched into Armenia; at Elegeia Parthamasiris laid his diadem at Trajan's feet expecting to receive it back, but Trajan annexed Armenia as a province, and Parthamasiris was killed on his way home. In 115 Trajan conquered northern Mesopotamia, receiving the submission of Abgar of Edessa and others, taking Nisibis and Batnae and earning the title Parthicus; he wintered at Antioch, where he survived the earthquake of December 115. In 116 he crossed the Tigris into Adiabene, created the provinces of Mesopotamia and Assyria, marched down the Euphrates to Babylon, captured Ctesiphon, taking Osroes's daughter and golden throne, and sailed to the Persian Gulf, regretting he was too old to follow Alexander to India. But revolts broke out behind him in Mesopotamia, Adiabene and Armenia, and the Jews of Mesopotamia rose at the same time as those of Cyrene, Egypt and Cyprus. Lusius Quietus, Erucius Clarus and Julius Alexander retook Nisibis, Edessa and Seleucia, and Trajan crowned the Parthian prince Parthamaspates as client king at Ctesiphon. In 117 he failed to take Hatra, fell ill and died in August at Selinus. Hadrian abandoned Mesopotamia, Assyria and most of Armenia and dismissed Parthamaspates, restoring the Euphrates frontier. Ancient writers (Dio, Fronto) attributed the war to Trajan's desire for glory; modern historians have suggested strategic aims (a defensible Tigris frontier), commercial motives (control of trade routes to the Gulf) or the need to resolve the Armenian question. Dio's epitome, Arrian's lost Parthica (in fragments), coins and inscriptions are the main sources.
set.debate: Motives: glory (Dio), strategic frontier, commerce or the Armenian question.

set.detail: The Diaspora revolt (115-117), known in rabbinic tradition as the "war of Qitos" (after Lusius Quietus), was a series of Jewish uprisings in Cyrenaica, Egypt, Cyprus and Mesopotamia during Trajan's Parthian war. In Cyrene in 115 the Jews, led by a "king" named Lukuas (or Andreas in Dio), attacked their Greek neighbours, destroying temples of Apollo, Zeus, Hecate and Artemis, the baths and roads, as inscriptions recording later Hadrianic restorations show; Dio's claim of 220,000 victims, with tales of cannibalism, is exaggerated. The revolt spread to Egypt, where Jewish forces fought Greeks and Roman troops in the countryside and besieged Alexandria; papyri record the anxiety of a strategos in Hermopolis and his family, the defeat of a Roman force, and later the confiscation of Jewish property and an annual festival at Oxyrhynchus commemorating the victory. In Cyprus, under Artemion, the Jews reportedly killed 240,000 people in Salamis and elsewhere, and Jews were afterwards forbidden to set foot on the island on pain of death. In Mesopotamia, Jews joined the general revolt against the Roman conquest, and Lusius Quietus suppressed them brutally. Trajan sent Quintus Marcius Turbo with land and naval forces to crush the revolt in Egypt and Cyrenaica, which took until 117. The Alexandrian community was destroyed, including its great synagogue, and Egyptian Jewry practically disappeared for two centuries; Cyrenaica was depopulated, and Hadrian founded a colony there (Hadrianopolis). Lusius Quietus became governor of Judaea, where some trouble may have occurred. Eusebius, Dio, Appian (an eyewitness who fled from the rebels in Egypt), papyri and inscriptions are the sources. The causes, possibly messianic expectations, tensions with Greek neighbours after 70 and the fiscus Judaicus, are debated, as is the connection with the Bar Kokhba war.
set.debate: Causes (messianism, communal conflict) and coordination of the revolts; the scale of casualties.

set.detail: The Bar Kokhba revolt (132-136) was the last great Jewish uprising against Rome. Led by Shimon bar Kosiba, styled "prince of Israel" (nasi) and hailed by some, including perhaps Rabbi Akiva, as the messiah, it broke out in 132 after Hadrian's decision to refound Jerusalem as Aelia Capitolina with a temple of Jupiter, or his ban on circumcision. The rebels used guerrilla tactics from underground hideouts and fortified villages and controlled much of Judaea, issuing their own coinage, often overstruck on Roman coins, and administering land through officials, as the letters from the Judaean desert show. The Roman governor Tineius Rufus and the Syrian legate Publicius Marcellus were unable to suppress the revolt, and Hadrian brought Sextus Julius Severus from Britain and troops from many provinces; X Fretensis and VI Ferrata were reinforced, and XXII Deiotariana may have been destroyed. Severus avoided pitched battles and wore down the rebels by besieging small groups and cutting off supplies. The war ended in 135 or 136 with the capture of Betar, south-west of Jerusalem, where Bar Kosiba died; rabbinic tradition placed the fall on 9 Av, the anniversary of the destruction of both Temples. Dio reports that 50 fortresses and 985 villages were destroyed and 580,000 men killed, besides countless deaths from famine and disease; Judaea was left almost depopulated. Refugees hid in caves near the Dead Sea, where letters and documents, including those of Babatha, were found. Jews were forbidden to enter Aelia, the province was renamed Syria Palaestina, and prisoners were sold so cheaply at the Terebinth market near Hebron that the price fell to that of a horse. Rabbinic tradition remembers the martyrdom of sages, including Akiva. Hadrian took a second imperatorial acclamation, and triumphal ornaments went to Severus, Marcellus and others. The revolt ended Jewish hopes of restoring the Temple for centuries and shifted the centre of Jewish life to Galilee and Babylonia.

The Roman-Parthian war of 161-166 was fought under Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus. Soon after Antoninus Pius's death in 161, Vologases IV of Parthia invaded Armenia and installed the Arsacid Pacorus as king; the governor of Cappadocia, Marcus Sedatius Severianus, encouraged by the prophet Alexander of Abonoteichus, advanced to Elegeia, where he was surrounded and killed with his legion (probably IX Hispana or XXII Deiotariana) after three days. The Parthians then invaded Syria and defeated its governor Attidius Cornelianus. In 162 Lucius Verus went east as commander-in-chief, establishing his base at Antioch, while Marcus stayed in Rome. Detachments from the Rhine and Danube, three legions (I Minervia, II Adiutrix, V Macedonica) and experienced generals were sent. Statius Priscus, transferred from Britain, captured Artaxata in 163 and established a new capital at Kainepolis for the Roman client Sohaemus. In 164-165 Avidius Cassius, commanding III Gallica, advanced down the Euphrates, defeated the Parthians at Dura-Europos, and captured Seleucia on the Tigris, which was sacked despite surrendering, and Ctesiphon, where the royal palace was burned; Martius Verus took Edessa, restoring its pro-Roman king Mannus, and Nisibis. In 166 Cassius invaded Media. The emperors took the titles Armeniacus, Parthicus Maximus and Medicus and celebrated a triumph in October 166. Rome kept control of north-western Mesopotamia, with Dura-Europos and Carrhae, and client kingdoms in Osroene and Armenia, preparing for the annexation of Mesopotamia under Severus. The army brought back the plague, which spread through the empire. Lucian satirised the flood of flattering histories of the war in How to Write History; Fronto planned a history of it, of which the preface survives. Dio's account survives only in fragments, and the Historia Augusta is unreliable.

The Marcomannic wars (166-180, with a continuation under Commodus until 182) were a series of conflicts on the middle Danube against the Marcomanni, Quadi, Iazyges and other peoples that dominated Marcus Aurelius's reign. Pressure from migrating peoples in the north (the Goths, Vandals and others) drove groups such as the Langobardi and Obii across the Danube in 166-167. In 168 Marcus and Lucius went to Aquileia; the plague devastated the army and Lucius died early in 169. Around 170 a Roman offensive failed, and the Marcomanni and Quadi under Ballomar invaded Italy, besieging Aquileia and destroying Opitergium, while the Costoboci raided Greece. Pompeianus and Pertinax drove the invaders out in 171, and Marcus established his headquarters at Carnuntum. In 172 the Romans crossed the Danube and defeated the Marcomanni (title Germanicus), with the "rain miracle" against the Quadi in 172 or 173 and the battle on the frozen Danube against the Iazyges. Peace was made with the Quadi and, in 175, with the Iazyges, who had to supply 8,000 cavalry, 5,500 of whom were sent to Britain; the revolt of Avidius Cassius interrupted operations. In 177-178 the war resumed (expeditio Germanica secunda), with Paternus's victory in 179 and 20,000 Roman troops stationed in forts in Marcomannic and Quadic territory, possibly as a prelude to new provinces of Marcomannia and Sarmatia. Marcus died in March 180, and Commodus made peace, imposing tribute, recruits, grain and restrictions on assemblies, but withdrawing the garrisons. The wars led to recruitment of slaves, gladiators and Germans, settlement of barbarians within the empire, debasement of the coinage, new legions (II and III Italica) and a reinforced defence of Italy. The Column of Marcus Aurelius depicts the campaigns. Modern historians see the wars as a turning point in relations between Rome and the peoples of central Europe, foreshadowing the crises of the third century.
